utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Will the Registry please bring in the accused? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, yes, hello. I would like to greet all the members and parties in this courtroom, as well as the interpreters. I assume everyone can hear me and that the technicians are working. Hello to everyone. Mr. Kehoe, we are going to then resume with Witness KK?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. President, I was having a problem with my equipment. We are going to continue with Witness KK. I believe the usher just went out to get him. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me? Can you hear me now? I am the one speaking to you now, it is the judges. First of all, please identify yourself, based on the document that will be put in front of you by the Registry. Look at your name. Do not say your name, just see if you recognise it. Please remain standing for a few moments longer so you can read the solemn declaration. WITNESS LL (Sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Please be seated. We are going to call you "Witness LL", because that corresponds to the protective measures which the Prosecutor has requested on your behalf. So, you are here to testify in the case of the Prosecution versus Mr. Blaskic, who is here in this courtroom. The judges ask that you speak without fear. You are under the protection of the International Criminal Tribunal. After a number of questions asked to you by the Prosecutor, then you will free to make your testimonies, talking about the things you have seen in your village and also about three or four other points. Perhaps there will be additional questions put to you by the judges, but, of course, you will also be asked questions by counsel for the accused during cross-examination. We are going to be sitting with you for about 30 minutes, we are not going to be able to finish. We ask for you to take a rest this evening and we will continue tomorrow afternoon with your testimony. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness LL, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of preliminary questions: did you live in the village of Gromiljak in Bosnia-Herzegovina until the 17th July 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived until 5th October of 1993, until I was exchanged and, on 17th July, I was thrown out of my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you of the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could briefly explain to the court the events that occurred in the town of Kiseljak after the multiparty elections in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness LL, when you respond to the questions, please, first of all, face the judges and also, can you come closer to the microphones so the interpreters can translate what you are saying? Thank you. Very well. Now you may answer the question put to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the multiparty elections in 1991 in Kiseljak, the HDZ won; that is, it won the most votes. Immediately the Croats started dominating. They first flew the Croatian flags on all public buildings and they imposed the Croatian language in schools. They also made the -- both the teachers and school children speak the Croatian dialect. They started instructing the Croatian population to have as little contact with the Muslims as possible and many children who -- many children who had socialised with us told us that they were forced to do that. So, the relations became very strained and were limited to business contacts at the minimum. Also, they were cutting us -- our phone lines, whereas the Croatian inhabitants did not have their lines cut off. We checked that with our Croatian neighbours. For instance, we would go there and ask them if their lines were open and they were at the time when we were receiving no signal. They also introduced the Croatian currency as the only official one, apart from the German currency, which was also used. The more educated people started saying that the Croats and Muslims could no longer live together, that Kiseljak was historically Croatian territory and it should be ethnically pure, and that Muslims should go to the towns where they were in majority, meaning Visoko, Zenica and they called it a "Muslim-mania" those two towns. A physician who was in town said, on several occasions, that all children that came from mixed marriages should be killed so that Kiseljak would be ethnically pure. They also set up Radio Kiseljak, where only Croats were employed; no Muslims were allowed to work there and anti-Muslim propaganda was spread through these broadcasts, often times they, sort of, broadcast these -- what they called revolutionary songs which were really very nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness LL, I do not want you to say your profession to the court because I do not want you to identify yourself, but would it be correct to say that you are a university-educated person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received higher education. At that time, my profession was still not available as through university courses, was not taught at universities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it would be right to say that you had had contact with a number of educated persons who were Bosnian Croats in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I worked in an institution where everybody did have education. We were over 100 and everybody was educated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you expressed your views a moment ago -- or expressed facts a moment ago -- about Croats, essentially saying that Muslims should leave the Kiseljak area and go to Zenica and Visoko, were these the views of educated Croats in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of other points on this area: were you aware of destruction being carried out on Muslim businesses in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew and I even saw -- I even saw some business premises which were destroyed, and this was especially the case when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started. The HVO army shot from their weapons into the Muslim shop windows. They looted some. I even saw a shoe shop which they vandalised. They tore out the protective grate that was there, and they looted everything. They also looted a butchers shop and then another shop. I also heard of similar cases elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were all Muslim-owned businesses in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you actually see the HVO carry out these acts, or did you just see the end result; the destroyed business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw what was left behind, what they had left behind and I saw that on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened to the Muslim relief agency, Merhamets in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. The Muslim organisation,, Merhamets, was set on fire and all the goods that were there were burned and then it was blown up, the building was blown up completely so the Muslims could not get any aid, any more, and they could not get it from Caritas organisation that was also in down. The two were completely separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who destroyed the Muslim relief agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that the HVO soldiers did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all of these events that you have testified to, happened prior to 18th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Merhamet was destroyed in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can move ahead in time to the attack on your village on 18th April 1993. If you could explain to the judges if you recall what happened on that day, from the beginning of 18th April? If you could go through to the period when you were allowed to return to your home by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th April in the morning, at 7.30 -- this was the Sunday, and it was a Catholic Easter holiday -- we heard shooting. My family was in the house and we heard the automatic weapons fire. It was a custom for the Catholics to shoot in the air on holidays as they were leaving church, so that is what we thought at first, but then we heard the heavy weapons detonations and then we realised that it was something else and not religious celebration. We did not have a basement in our house, so my family and another family from my neighbourhood moved into a house of another neighbour who did have a basement. We were a total of eight and we were all civilians. A short while later, a car arrived and three HVO soldiers jumped out of the car. This was in front of our house and they -- they requested that we let them in with their weapons pointed at us. We did and they said that they came to get the weapons, so they told us to surrender the weapons. We told them that we did not have them. Then they said they would search the house and if they found the weapons, then we would be killed and our house set on fire. They searched the entire house from the attic to the basement and, after not having found anything, they left. Shortly thereafter, another four HVO soldiers came and they did the same thing. They searched every house in the neighbourhood and this was repeated several times over the next several days. They searched all houses in the neighbourhood. We, again, heard detonations thereafter and looked out the window. Then we saw, in the immediate vicinity, houses on fire. This was the village of Visnjica and at 1.00 pm there was an old couple's house, they were retired, they did not have any sons or any military there. Their house was set on fire first and it was followed by some other houses. Round 4.00 a man, a neighbour, came from the village and he told us that he came on orders of the Chief of Police. He came to tell us that we had to report to a basement of a house at 6.00. If we did not do that, that they would come and arrest us. We went to this basement at 6.00 and we found a large number of civilians there who were of Muslim ethnic background. Then a group of HVO policemen arrived, who separated out the men and took them to another basement, which was away from this house. We had a pregnant woman in our house. She was about to give birth. I asked that we women be released so that we could go back home. However, they did not allow that, but that evening they put us up in a house of a Croat, where we were supposed to stay the night. The next day they released us home, only for women, and in the basement where the men were, there were 63 persons of Muslim ethnic background. The conditions were such that there was no floor there, there was just rubbish, some wood and some rocks. There were small children among them, including some babies. They had no food, no water and in front of the basement there were armed HVO soldiers who guarded them so they would not escape. After seven days, women and children were released, while the men were kept there for 15 days and every day they would take them to dig trenches. After that, they released them home, but they had to report to the police every morning and every evening. After 15 days when the situation seemed to have calmed down, I returned to work to see whether I was going to be able to continue to work there. I was allowed to come back to work, as were the others, but before that, we had to receive a permission from the HVO authorities. I had to go on foot for six kilometres to get to work every day, because no bus or taxi cab wanted to stop and give me a ride. On 24th May in the evening, since curfew was introduced for Muslims which lasted between 21.00 until 05.00 hours, three HVO soldiers came and knocked on the door. I did not want to open up because I was alone in the house. Members of my family managed to escape to the free territory by 20th May, so I was the only one left in the house to guard it and to continue working. I managed to hide among the plants on the balcony and I spent the entire night there. I saw and heard what was going on in front of my house during the night. They were talking about how they needed to take my son's car as well as my neighbour's car and how they were going to kill my neighbour the next day when they catch him. Then they killed my dog. If I need to give names, I know all the names of the people who were involved. In the morning, since the curfew was until 05.00, after the HVO soldiers, who were standing guard in front of my house, after they withdrew, I warned my neighbour that they had decided to kill him and since there was fog -- it was early in the morning -- he managed to escape across the hills to the free territory. That day I went to work and I went to the police headquarters to see the chief and I told him what had transpired the night before, but he did nothing. When I came back home, the door to the apartment had been broken down and my son's vehicle was gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, everything has been re-established. You may continue for a few more minutes, then it is up to the Prosecutor to decide when to stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked a man to have the lock fixed, exchanged, so that I remained in the house. On 27th May, as I was coming back from work with a colleague of mine, I saw a man I knew driving my son's car in downtown Kiseljak, and he was parking the car across the street from the Kiseljak police station. I approached the vehicle and I asked him to please return the car, at which point he opened the door; he pushed me aside and started beating me savagely. About 10 HVO policemen stood around watching all this, they were maybe a metre or two away from us, and they were laughing openly. He beat me up; he insulted me and he spat at me. After that, I went to the UNPROFOR base, where the Canadian contingent was staying and, since I can communicate in English, I told them what had happened to me. The soldier called the command in Visoko and told them about it, and the next day an officer came from Visoko. He took my statement and several other neighbours also used this opportunity, and these were people who were also abused by the HVO soldiers. So they also lodged complaints. The Canadian officer promised that he would come again and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that is probably a good time to pause until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, we shall stop here. This will give the time for the witness to relax and to give a break. So the Chamber now stands adjourned. Tomorrow is the last afternoon of the week, as you know. I make this statement to the Prosecution and to the Defence. Tomorrow we will resume at 2.30 pm. The Chamber stands adjourned. (6.30 pm)
